extracted.intended_audience: writers and speakers seeking guidance on eloquence, style, persuasion, and arrangement of discourse
extracted.subtask_description: Practical guidance for composing and delivering persuasive, natural, and well-ordered prose or speeches — covering audience adaptation, word choice, arrangement, simplicity, and moral tone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eloquence as correspondence between head and heart
rubrics_metrics.description: Eloquence consists in establishing a correspondence between the head and the heart of those to whom we speak and between our thoughts and expressions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make the hearer listen without pain and with pleasure; aim that self-love leads the audience to reflect willingly. (Original: 'It consists, then, in a correspondence which we seek to establish between the head and the heart...')

rubrics_metrics.name: Study the audience by trial on your own heart
rubrics_metrics.description: We must put ourselves in the place of those who are to hear us, and make trial on our own heart of the turn which we give to our discourse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anticipate how the intended audience will receive phrasing and emotional tone by checking whether the discourse moves your own heart — adjust accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pleasantness must be drawn from the true
rubrics_metrics.description: Eloquence requires the pleasant and the real; but the pleasant must itself be drawn from the true.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid ornament or charm that lacks truth; persuasive beauty should rest on accurate content, not elaborate falsehoods or mere cleverness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simplicity and suitability to the subject
rubrics_metrics.description: We ought to restrict ourselves, so far as possible, to the simple and natural, and not to magnify that which is little, or belittle that which is great. It is not enough that a thing be beautiful; it must be suitable to the subject, and there must be in it nothing of excess or defect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Match tone and style to subject matter; avoid exaggeration or understatement; prefer natural expression over showy devices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Persuade by sweetness rather than authority
rubrics_metrics.description: Eloquence, which persuades by sweetness, not by authority; as a tyrant, not as a king.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor gentle, attractive persuasion that engages the listener's goodwill rather than relying on domineering or purely authoritative claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paint thought; avoid over-ornamentation
rubrics_metrics.description: Eloquence is a painting of thought; and thus those who, after having painted it, add something more, make a picture instead of a portrait.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Once thought is clearly expressed, do not pile on gratuitous embellishments that distract from the original idea.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid forced antitheses and artificial figures
rubrics_metrics.description: Those who make antitheses by forcing words are like those who make false windows for symmetry. Their rule is not to speak accurately, but to make apt figures of speech.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not prioritize rhetorical neatness or clever contrasts over accuracy and natural expression; avoid constructions that are merely ornamental.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer natural style to affected artistry
rubrics_metrics.description: When we see a natural style, we are astonished and delighted; for we expected to see an author, and we find a man.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for a voice that feels human and direct rather than ostentatiously 'literary' or showy; authenticity delights readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beauty of omission and uprightness
rubrics_metrics.description: We only consult the ear because the heart is wanting. The rule is uprightness. Beauty of omission, of judgment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Know what to leave unstated; elegant restraint and moral uprightness in tone often serve better than excessive elaboration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Word order and arrangement change meaning
rubrics_metrics.description: Words differently arranged have a different meaning, and meanings differently arranged have different effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be deliberate with syntax and sequence; rearranging words or ideas can alter both sense and persuasive force.

rubrics_metrics.name: Repetition is allowable when appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: When we find words repeated in a discourse, and, in trying to correct them, discover that they are so appropriate that we would spoil the discourse, we must leave them alone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don't remove repetition reflexively; if repetition serves emphasis or natural rhythm, preserve it rather than correcting for variety's sake.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use names and titles appropriately — don't mask nature
rubrics_metrics.description: To mask nature and disguise her. No more king, pope, bishop--but 'august monarch', etc.; not Paris--'the capital of the kingdom'. There are places in which we ought to call Paris, Paris, and others in which we ought to call it the capital of the kingdom.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose naming and epithets suitable to context; avoid inflated or euphemistic labels where plain terms are better.

rubrics_metrics.name: Word choice gives dignity to meaning; use examples
rubrics_metrics.description: The same meaning changes with the words which express it. Meanings receive their dignity from words instead of giving it to them. Examples should be sought....
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select words that lend appropriate dignity or tone to ideas; illustrate abstract claims with concrete examples to give them weight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Humility in attribution (avoid 'my book')
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain authors... say, 'My book,' 'My commentary,' 'My history,' etc. ... They would do better to say, 'Our book,' 'Our commentary,' 'Our history,' etc., because there is in them usually more of other people's than their own.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt modesty in speaking of one's work; acknowledge influences and shared contributions rather than claiming undue ownership.

rubrics_metrics.name: Silence can promote favorable opinion
rubrics_metrics.description: Do you wish people to believe good of you? Don't speak.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When attempting to appear admirable, restraint or silence is often more effective than self-praise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid over-apologizing and unnecessary excuses
rubrics_metrics.description: I always feel uncomfortable under such compliments as these: 'I have given you a great deal of trouble,' 'I am afraid I am boring you,' 'I fear this is too long.' We either carry our audience with us, or irritate them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don't preemptively apologize or undercut your speech; either engage your audience fully or risk annoying them by solicitous disclaimers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid luxuriant, grandiose phrasing
rubrics_metrics.description: 'To extinguish the torch of sedition'; too luxuriant. 'The restlessness of his genius'; two superfluous grand words.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reject inflated metaphors and pompous diction that do not serve clarity or truth; prefer precise and fitting language.

rubrics_metrics.name: Order matters but avoid artificial containment
rubrics_metrics.description: Nature has made all her truths independent of one another. Our art makes one dependent on the other. But this is not natural. Each keeps its own place.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Organize material so truths appear naturally; avoid forcing an artificial hierarchy of divisions that conceals rather than clarifies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decide content order after drafting
rubrics_metrics.description: The last thing one settles in writing a book is what one should put in first.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write freely during composition; determine the optimal front-to-back ordering once material is fully developed.

rubrics_metrics.name: When correcting others, begin by acknowledging their true viewpoint
rubrics_metrics.description: When we wish to correct with advantage, and to show another that he errs, we must notice from what side he views the matter, for on that side it is usually true, and admit that truth to him, but reveal to him the side on which it is false.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Start by conceding the valid aspects of the interlocutor's position before introducing corrections; this reduces offense and opens receptivity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Favor persuasion by self-discovery
rubrics_metrics.description: People are generally better persuaded by the reasons which they have themselves discovered than by those which have come into the mind of others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Structure argument and questioning so that readers/listeners arrive at conclusions themselves rather than feeling lectured; Socratic elenchus and guided discovery are effective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Natural discourse evokes pre-existing truth in the reader
rubrics_metrics.description: When a natural discourse paints a passion or an effect, one feels within oneself the truth of what one reads, which was there before, although one did not know it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim to reveal or mirror feelings and intuitions the audience already has; persuasion that makes readers 'recognize' their own thought is powerful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid treating intuitive matters with excessive formalism
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematicians wish to treat matters of intuition mathematically...they make themselves ridiculous, wishing to begin with definitions and then with axioms, which is not the way to proceed in this kind of reasoning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When addressing subjects grasped by intuition, do not over-formalize with dry definitions and axioms; allow tacit, felt judgments their place.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be broadly informed rather than narrowly learned
rubrics_metrics.description: If we cannot be universal and know all that is to be known of everything, we ought to know a little about everything. For it is far better to know something about everything than to know all about one thing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cultivate general knowledge to adapt to varied audiences and contexts; breadth often serves speakers better than narrow specialization in social discourse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use particular examples to prove general rules and vice versa
rubrics_metrics.description: Thus when we wish to demonstrate a general theorem, we must give the rule as applied to a particular case; but if we wish to demonstrate a particular case, we must begin with the general rule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose explanatory direction according to what is obscure: use concrete instances to illuminate general claims, and general framing to situate particulars.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid being labeled by a single specialty; aim for universality in manner
rubrics_metrics.description: We should not be able to say of a man, 'He is a mathematician,' or 'a preacher,' or 'eloquent'; but that he is 'a gentleman.' That universal quality alone pleases me.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Present oneself as adaptable and generally serviceable rather than narrowly defined by one skill; versatility is valuable in social discourse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use common errors or familiar notions cautiously to orient readers
rubrics_metrics.description: When we do not know the truth of a thing, it is of advantage that there should exist a common error which determines the mind of man... For the chief malady of man is restless curiosity about things which he cannot understand; and it is not so bad for him to be in error as to be curious to no purpose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When truth is obscure, invoking shared, accessible beliefs can stabilize comprehension — but be careful not to perpetuate falsehoods where correction is possible.
